summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application (DAO layer, views, middlewares, auth utils, app setup, routes, templates, config and migrations). This is an intentionally vulnerable app and the code confirms it: a classic SQL injection in Student.create, global disabling of Jinja2 autoescaping leading to stored XSS, CSRF protection written but not wired in, weak unsalted MD5 password hashing, session cookies without HttpOnly, and missing authentication/authorization on all state-changing endpoints. Overall risk is critical. Coverage was the full Python source tree plus templates and config; static JS/CSS assets and font files were not reviewed.

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via string-formatted INSERT
findings.description: Student.create builds its INSERT by Python %-formatting the user-supplied name directly into the SQL string instead of passing it as a bound parameter. The value comes straight from the unauthenticated POST /students/ handler (views.py:54-57, data['name']), so any anonymous visitor can inject arbitrary SQL. A payload like  x'); DROP TABLE marks;-- , or a stacked query using psycopg2, allows reading/altering any table (including the users table with password hashes) or destroying data. The sibling DAO methods (Course.create, Review.create, Mark.create, the get/get_many methods) correctly use bound parameters; this is the one that does not.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  then  await cur.execute(q). Source: views.students -> data = await request.post(); await Student.create(conn, data['name']).
findings.recommendation: Pass parameters to the driver instead of formatting them in: q = "INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)"; await cur.execute(q, {'name': name}). Never build SQL with % / f-strings on untrusted input.

findings.title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. User-controlled values persisted through the app are rendered verbatim: course review text ({{ review.review_text }}, course.jinja2:22), course title/description (course.jinja2:14-15), and student name ({{ name }}, students.jinja2:16). An unauthenticated attacker can POST a review containing <script>...</script> (views.review:119-129 has no sanitization) which then executes in every visitor's browser when the course page is viewed, enabling session/credential theft. Because session cookies are not HttpOnly (see separate finding), the stolen cookie is directly readable by the injected script.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Templates emit {{ review.review_text }}, {{ course.title }}, {{ course.description }}, {{ name }} with no |e filter.
findings.recommendation: Remove autoescape=False (default to autoescape=True / select_autoescape(['html','jinja2'])), and only mark genuinely trusted HTML with |safe where needed.

findings.title: CSRF protection implemented but not enabled
findings.description: The application defines a working csrf_middleware (middlewares.py:25-38) and a csrf_token context processor, and templates emit a hidden _csrf_token field, but the middleware is commented out of the Application middleware list, so CSRF tokens are never validated on POST. Every state-changing endpoint (create student, create course, submit review, evaluate/grade a student, login, logout) accepts cross-site forged POSTs. An attacker page can silently create reviews (delivering the stored XSS above), create students/courses, or submit grades on behalf of a logged-in admin.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware]  -- csrf_middleware is commented out. csrf_middleware in middlewares.py:28-37 does pop token and compare, but is never registered.
findings.recommendation: Add csrf_middleware to the middlewares list so it runs on all POST requests, and ensure every form includes the token (it already does in most templates).

findings.title: Weak unsalted MD5 password hashing
findings.description: Passwords are verified (and, per migrations/001-fixtures.sql, stored) as unsalted single-round MD5 hashes. MD5 is fast and broken: if the users table is dumped (e.g. via the SQL injection above) the hashes fall instantly to rainbow tables / GPU cracking, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. The fixtures seed md5('superadmin') for the admin and md5('password') for other users, confirming the scheme in use. The comparison is also a non-constant-time == comparison.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(); fixtures: pwd_hash values are md5('superadmin'), md5('password'), md5('spidey').
findings.recommendation: Use a memory-hard adaptive hash (argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt) with a per-user salt, and compare with the library's constant-time verifier. Rehash existing passwords on next login.

findings.title: Session cookie configured without HttpOnly flag
findings.description: The Redis session storage is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is accessible to client-side JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS from disabled autoescaping, this lets an injected script read document.cookie and exfiltrate the session identifier, directly hijacking authenticated (including admin) sessions. The Secure flag is also not set.
findings.recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default), set secure=True when served over HTTPS, and consider samesite='Lax'/'Strict'.

findings.title: Missing authentication/authorization on state-changing endpoints
findings.description: The evaluate handler, which creates grade marks for a student, performs no authentication or admin check before calling Mark.create, so any anonymous user who POSTs to /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} can assign grades. The authorize() decorator exists (utils/auth.py:12-23) but is only applied to logout. The same missing-check pattern affects the other mutating handlers: students create (views.py:54-57), courses create (views.py:86-90), and review create (views.py:119-129) are all reachable unauthenticated. The templates only hide the admin UI via {% if auth_user.is_admin %}, which is cosmetic and does not enforce access control at the route.
findings.evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... data = await request.post(); ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']) -- no @authorize(ensure_admin=True). Only logout uses @authorize().
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize()/@authorize(ensure_admin=True) to every mutating handler as appropriate, enforcing the check server-side rather than only in templates.

findings.title: aiohttp application runs with debug=True
findings.description: The Application is constructed with debug=True unconditionally (not driven by configuration/environment). In debug mode aiohttp/asyncio enables extra diagnostics and more verbose error surfaces, which can leak internal details in a production deployment and is not something that should be hardcoded on.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production.

findings.title: Hardcoded default credentials in config and fixtures
findings.description: The default config ships database credentials postgres/**** in plaintext, and this is the default config path used by app.init (default_config='./config/dev.yaml'). In addition, migrations/001-fixtures.sql seeds an administrative account 'superadmin' with the trivial password 'superadmin' and other accounts with 'password'. If these defaults are carried into any non-local deployment they constitute known credentials an attacker can use directly. These look like development/demo values rather than live production secrets, but they should not be reachable in production.
findings.evidence: config/dev.yaml db: user: postgres / password: ****. migrations/001-fixtures.sql: ('Super',...,'superadmin', md5('superadmin'), TRUE).
findings.recommendation: Load secrets from environment/secret manager, never commit real credentials, and do not seed privileged accounts with guessable passwords; force a password change on first login for any seeded admin.
